children.label: Overview
children: Shared MOA → β-lactam ring binds penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) → blocks peptidoglycan (D-alanyl-D-alanine) cross-linking → bactericidal. Bacterial β-lactamases (often plasmid-encoded) cleave the ring → resistance.

children.label: Natural Penicillins — Penicillin G, Penicillin V
children: Penicillin V → oral, acid-stable, poor bioavailability → minor infections only (e.g., streptococcal pharyngitis)
Penicillin G → IV/IM administration
Pen G or V → rheumatic fever; Pen G → intrapartum GBS prophylaxis; single-dose benzathine Pen G → syphilis
Covers → Staph, Strep, Neisseria meningitidis, Actinomyces israelii, Clostridium perfringens (gangrene), Pasteurella (dog bites)
Strep viridans / Strep bovis → subacute left-sided endocarditis
AE → Type I IgE hypersensitivity; drug-induced autoimmune hemolytic anemia (+ direct Coombs); interstitial nephritis
Resistance → β-lactamases (plasmid-encoded)

children.label: Antistaphylococcal Penicillins — Nafcillin, Oxacillin
children: Bulky R-groups → resist β-lactamase cleavage → narrow spectrum, staphylococci only
Uses → skin/soft tissue infections (folliculitis, abscess); staph endocarditis; staph osteomyelitis
AE → same as penicillin
MRSA → resistance via altered PBP (not β-lactamase-mediated) → resistant to all β-lactams, including nafcillin/oxacillin

children.label: Aminopenicillins — Amoxicillin, Ampicillin
children: Extended gram-negative coverage; susceptible to β-lactamases → often paired with clavulanate
Amoxicillin (oral, good bioavailability) → otitis media / sinusitis (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis); strep throat (+ ampicillin); pneumonia (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, + ampicillin)
Amoxicillin → part of H. pylori triple therapy (+ clarithromycin + PPI); Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi)
Amoxicillin prophylaxis → asplenic patients (encapsulated organisms: S. pneumoniae, H. flu); high-risk dental procedures (endocarditis prevention)
Ampicillin → IV; covers enterococcus; meningitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes; GI/urinary gram-negative rods
Resistance → ampicillin-resistant enterococcus strains via β-lactamase production
AE → Stevens-Johnson syndrome (rash); drug-induced liver injury; rash with EBV/infectious mononucleosis

children.label: Antipseudomonal Penicillins & β-Lactamase Inhibitors
children: Piperacillin, Ticarcillin → paired with β-lactamase inhibitors (prevents cleavage) → cover anaerobes + Pseudomonas
β-lactamase inhibitors → clavulanate, sulbactam, tazobactam (no intrinsic antibacterial activity; extend coverage of partner drug)

children.label: Cephalosporins (1st–5th Generation)
children: Gen: 1st | Drugs: Cephalexin, Cefazolin | Coverage: Gram (+): staph, strep; some gram (–): Proteus, E. coli, Klebsiella | Key Uses: Cellulitis, abscess, S. pyogenes; cefazolin → surgical prophylaxis
Gen: 2nd | Drugs: Cefuroxime, Cefotetan, Cefoxitin | Coverage: 1st gen + H. flu, Neisseria, Serratia ("HENS") | Key Uses: Extended gram-negative coverage vs 1st gen

Gen: 3rd | Drugs: Ceftriaxone, Cefotaxime, Ceftazidime | Coverage: Extended gram (–) beyond 2nd gen | Key Uses: Meningitis (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime); CAP/HAP; single-dose IM ceftriaxone → gonorrhea; Lyme disease; ceftazidime → Pseudomonas; ceftriaxone → endocarditis (strep viridans, HACEK)
Gen: 4th | Drugs: Cefepime | Coverage: Broad spectrum + Pseudomonas | Key Uses: Bacterial meningitis
Gen: 5th | Drugs: Ceftaroline | Coverage: Broad spectrum | Key Uses: MRSA infections
AE → same as penicillin (hypersensitivity, hemolytic anemia, interstitial nephritis); cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy
Resistance → most β-lactamases ineffective vs cephalosporins; resistance via altered PBPs + extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs)

children.label: Monobactams — Aztreonam
children: Covers → aerobic gram-negative rods only (no gram-positive/anaerobe activity)
Uses → serious gram-negative infections (meningitis, pneumonia, sepsis); Pseudomonas
Safe in patients with penicillin allergy (no cross-reactivity)
Resistant to β-lactamases

children.label: Carbapenems — Imipenem, Meropenem, Ertapenem, Doripenem
children: Broadest-spectrum β-lactams; resistant to extended-spectrum β-lactamases
Uses → multidrug-resistant infections; anaerobes (aspiration pneumonia, intra-abdominal infection); Pseudomonas
Imipenem → inactivated by renal dehydropeptidase → paired with cilastatin (inhibits dehydropeptidase, prevents degradation)
AE → GI upset; skin rash; imipenem lowers seizure threshold

children.label: Overview
children: MOA → inserts lipid tail into gram-positive cell membrane → depolarization → cell death
Covers → Staph (incl. MRSA), Strep, Enterococcus (incl. VRE)
Uses → MRSA bacteremia; staph endocarditis
Ineffective for pneumonia (inactivated by pulmonary surfactant)
AE → myopathy, rare rhabdomyolysis → monitor CPK

children.label: 30S Inhibitors — Tetracyclines
children: MOA → irreversible binding to 30S subunit → blocks tRNA attachment; broad spectrum
Covers → MRSA; tick-borne organisms (Rickettsia, Ehrlichia, Francisella, Borrelia); Brucella; culture-negative endocarditis (Coxiella); Yersinia
Covers → Chlamydia (cervicitis, urethritis, PID, atypical pneumonia); Mycoplasma ("walking" pneumonia); acne
AE → tooth discoloration / bone deposition in children; photosensitivity; GI upset; Fanconi syndrome (type 2 RTA, with expired tetracyclines)
Divalent/trivalent cations (Ca, Fe, Mg) → chelation → ↓ absorption
Resistance → efflux pumps, ribosomal alteration. Eliminated fecally → safe in renal failure

children.label: 30S Inhibitors — Aminoglycosides
children: MOA → irreversible binding to 30S → blocks initiation complex, causes mRNA misreading; bactericidal
Uptake is O2-dependent → no activity vs anaerobes; often combined with a cell-wall agent (β-lactam/vancomycin) for synergy (e.g., enterococcus)
AE → nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis); ototoxicity (vestibular/cochlear); teratogenic (fetal deafness)
Contraindication → myasthenia gravis (post-NMJ blockade)
Drug: Streptomycin | Distinguishing Feature: Tularemia (Francisella), plague (Yersinia pestis)
Drug: Gentamicin | Distinguishing Feature: Resistant gram-negatives (Enterobacter, Serratia, Klebsiella); septicemia; Pseudomonas
Drug: Tobramycin | Distinguishing Feature: + cell-wall agent → enterococcus; inactivated by E. faecium acetylation enzyme
Drug: Amikacin | Distinguishing Feature: Retains activity vs E. faecium with acetylation enzymes (escapes tobramycin resistance)
Drug: Neomycin | Distinguishing Feature: Stays active in GI tract, excreted in feces → bowel prep before colorectal surgery

children.label: 50S Inhibitors — Macrolides (Azithromycin, Clarithromycin, Erythromycin)
children: MOA → bind 50S subunit → block translocation; bacteriostatic
Uses → CAP (S. pneumoniae, H. flu, M. catarrhalis); atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Legionella); Chlamydia pneumoniae/trachomatis
Uses → pertussis (Bordetella) + prophylaxis for contacts; Bartonella; Mycobacterium avium (MAC) + prophylaxis at CD4 <50
Oral erythromycin → neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis & pneumonia; erythromycin drops → neonatal conjunctivitis prophylaxis vs N. gonorrhoeae; erythromycin → diphtheria
Clarithromycin → part of H. pylori triple therapy (+ amoxicillin + PPI)
Safe alternative in penicillin allergy
AE → ↑ GI motility; acute cholestatic jaundice; QT prolongation; CYP450 inhibition

children.label: 50S Inhibitors — Clindamycin
children: MOA → binds 50S → blocks translocation; bacteriostatic
Covers → Staph, Strep (GAS, cellulitis, soft tissue infection), MRSA; anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, C. perfringens)

Uses → aspiration pneumonia, deep-seated abscesses (excellent penetration); bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella); + gentamicin → polymicrobial female genital tract infection; topical → moderate-severe inflammatory acne; + atovaquone → babesiosis
"Clindamycin above the diaphragm, metronidazole below" — anaerobic coverage split
AE → diarrhea → C. diff pseudomembranous colitis

children.label: 50S Inhibitors — Chloramphenicol
children: MOA → reversible binding to 50S → blocks peptide bond formation; bacteriostatic
Uses → empiric meningitis in developing countries (S. pneumo, H. flu, N. meningitidis); alternative agent for serious rickettsial infection (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) — safe in pregnancy
AE → dose-related reversible anemia; aplastic anemia; gray baby syndrome (neonates lack glucuronidation → flaccidity, hypothermia, shock)

children.label: 50S Inhibitors — Linezolid
children: MOA → reversible binding to 50S → blocks initiation complex; bacteriostatic
Covers → gram-positive only: Staph (incl. MRSA), Strep, Enterococcus (incl. VRE)
Uses → serious gram-positive infections; nosocomial MRSA pneumonia
AE → thrombocytopenia; peripheral/optic neuropathy; serotonin syndrome (weak MAOI activity)

children.label: Sulfamethoxazole / Trimethoprim (TMP-SMX)
children: MOA → PABA → [SMX blocks dihydropteroate synthetase] → dihydrofolic acid → [TMP blocks dihydrofolate reductase] → tetrahydrofolic acid → purines/DNA
Uses → 1st-line UTI; acute prostatitis; PJP treatment + prophylaxis at CD4 <200; Nocardia; MRSA skin infections
Pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine → toxoplasmosis treatment; TMP-SMX prophylaxis for toxoplasmosis at CD4 <100
AE → pancytopenia/megaloblastic anemia; teratogen (neural tube defects, 1st trimester); sulfa allergy (fever, urticaria, rash, SJS)
AE → hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency; type IV RTA (hyperkalemia); interstitial nephritis; photosensitivity
AE → kernicterus in neonate (if used in last month of pregnancy — displaces bilirubin); displaces warfarin from albumin → bleeding; drug-induced lupus; CYP450 inhibition

children.label: Fluoroquinolones — Ciprofloxacin, Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin
children: MOA → inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase); mainly gram-negative coverage
Uses → gram-negative UTI (E. coli, Proteus), incl. complicated UTI/pyelonephritis (Pseudomonas); prostatitis
Uses → gastroenteritis (Shigella, Salmonella, E. coli) — ↑ risk of Salmonella osteomyelitis in sickle cell patients; anthrax (B. anthracis)
Respiratory quinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) → CAP (S. pneumoniae); atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Legionella)
AE → QT prolongation; GI upset; tendon rupture (elderly, steroid users); cartilage damage — teratogenic, avoid in children <10 yrs and pregnancy
Divalent/trivalent cations → ↓ absorption

children.label: Metronidazole
children: MOA → forms free radicals → disrupts bacterial/protozoal DNA; bactericidal
Covers → anaerobes (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Clostridium incl. C. diff); protozoa (Entamoeba histolytica — liver abscess, Giardia, Trichomonas)

Uses → intra-abdominal infections; bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella); trichomonal vaginitis/cervicitis (treat partner too); C. diff colitis; substitute for amoxicillin in H. pylori triple therapy (penicillin allergy)
"Metronidazole below the diaphragm" — complements clindamycin's anaerobic coverage
AE → disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (flushing, tachycardia, N/V)

children.label: Overview
children: RIPE regimen (active TB) → Rifampin + Isoniazid + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol × 2 months → then Isoniazid + Rifampin × 4 months (prevents resistance development).

Drug: Isoniazid (INH) | MOA: Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (cell wall); activated by catalase-peroxidase (KatG) | Key AE: Peripheral neuropathy (↓B6); hepatotoxicity; drug-induced lupus; seizures; anion gap metabolic acidosis
Drug: Rifampin | MOA: Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase | Key AE: Hepatotoxic; orange body fluids
Drug: Pyrazinamide | MOA: — | Key AE: Hyperuricemia → gout, needle-shaped uric acid crystals; hepatotoxic
Drug: Ethambutol | MOA: Blocks arabinosyl transferase (cell wall carbohydrate synthesis) | Key AE: Optic neuritis (↓ visual acuity, red-green color blindness)

INH → resistance via ↓KatG; metabolized by hepatic N-acetyltransferase — slow acetylators → ↑ risk of side effects; give with pyridoxine (B6) to prevent neuropathy; inhibits CYP450; used alone for latent TB
Rifampin → activates CYP450 (opposite of INH); resistance develops rapidly if used alone; prophylaxis for close contacts of H. flu and N. meningitidis
All RIPE drugs → hepatotoxic

children.label: Mycobacterium avium Complex (MAC)
children: Common cause of disseminated disease in AIDS patients
Treatment → macrolide (azithromycin/clarithromycin) + ethambutol ± rifabutin (3rd agent)
Prophylaxis → macrolide when CD4 <50
Rifampin and rifabutin → activate CYP450

children.label: Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae)
children: Dapsone → AE: hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency (bite cells, Heinz bodies); agranulocytosis
Clofazimine → treats lepromatous leprosy (leonine facies)
Rifampin → also used to treat leprosy

children.label: Amphotericin B
children: MOA → binds ergosterol in fungal membrane → forms pores → cell death
Toxicity → non-selective binding to mammalian cholesterol membranes (basis of AE)
Resistance → ↓ ergosterol content in membrane
Uses → severe systemic fungal infections; IV (liposomal formulation available); intrathecal for fungal CNS infections
AE → hypotension, headache; infusion reaction ("shake and bake" fevers/chills); seizures/CNS effects; thrombophlebitis
AE → renal tubular acidosis type 1; hypokalemia; renal Mg wasting; anemia (↓ EPO production)
Pre-treatment → IV normal saline volume expansion before dosing (↓ nephrotoxicity)

children.label: Flucytosine
children: MOA → fluorinated cytosine → converted by cytosine deaminase → 5-fluorouracil → halts fungal DNA/RNA synthesis
Uses → combined with amphotericin B → treats Cryptococcus

children.label: Nystatin
children: MOA → same as amphotericin (binds ergosterol → membrane pores)
Covers → Candida
Uses → mucocutaneous/vaginal candidiasis; oral rinse for oral candidiasis

children.label: Azoles
children: MOA → inhibit lanosterol → ergosterol conversion via CYP450 inhibition
Class effect → all azoles prone to drug interactions

children.label: Azoles › Voriconazole
children: Strong CYP450 inhibitor → dose-reduce cyclosporine, tacrolimus, statins
AE → visual disturbances (blurry vision, flashes of light, color vision changes)
Uses → invasive aspergillosis; candida esophagitis (AIDS patients)

children.label: Azoles › Fluconazole
children: Uses → Candida infections (mucocutaneous); one-time oral dose → vaginal candidiasis; systemic → candida stomatitis/esophagitis
Uses → cryptococcal meningitis (high CNS penetration)

children.label: Azoles › Itraconazole
children: Uses → systemic dimorphic fungi (histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, sporothrix)
Uses → onychomycosis, dermatophytosis

children.label: Azoles › Clotrimazole & Miconazole
children: Topical → tinea infections
Combined → vaginal candidiasis

children.label: Azoles › Ketoconazole
children: Topical → dermatomycosis
Inhibits 17,20-desmolase (1st step of steroid synthesis from cholesterol) → ↓ androgens/estrogens; ↓ adrenal cortisol overproduction (Cushing disease)
AE → anti-androgenic effects (gynecomastia)

children.label: Griseofulvin & Terbinafine — Dermatophyte Agents
children: Griseofulvin → binds fungal microtubules → halts metaphase; activates CYP450; oral → dermatophytosis (tinea corporis/pedis/cruris)
Terbinafine → inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase → squalene accumulation; topical → dermatophytes; oral → onychomycosis; AE → GI effects, hepatotoxicity
Oral griseofulvin + terbinafine → first-line for tinea capitis in children

children.label: Echinocandins — Caspofungin, Micafungin, Anidulafungin
children: MOA → inhibit β-1,3-glucan synthesis in fungal cell wall (NOT membrane, NOT ergosterol)
Covers → excellent activity vs Candida
Uses → IV only; systemic candida infections, esophageal candidiasis, invasive aspergillus

children.label: HIV Life Cycle & Drug Targets
children: Infects → CD4+ T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells
gag gene → core proteins (p24, p7)
env gene → envelope proteins gp120 and gp41 (sent to ER first)
gp120 → binds host CD4 + coreceptor (CXCR4/CCR5) → viral entry
gp41 → mediates membrane fusion
POL gene → encodes protease, reverse transcriptase, integrase; mutation → resistance to NRTIs, NNRTIs, PIs, AND integrase inhibitors

children.label: NRTIs — Nucleoside/Nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors
children: MOA → lack 3'-OH → block 3'-5' phosphodiester bond formation → incorporated into viral DNA → chain termination
Require phosphorylation by cellular enzymes for activation (exception: tenofovir)
Suffix → "-dine"
AE (class) → mitochondrial toxicity → lactic acidosis
Drug: Lamivudine | Distinguishing Feature: + tenofovir → treats Hep B; (+ stavudine, didanosine) → peripheral neuropathy
Drug: Tenofovir | Distinguishing Feature: Already a nucleotide → no phosphorylation needed; + lamivudine → Hep B
Drug: Zidovudine (AZT) | Distinguishing Feature: Used in pregnancy/breastfeeding → ↓ vertical transmission; AE: myelosuppression, anemia, agranulocytopenia; (+ stavudine) → lipodystrophy
Drug: Stavudine | Distinguishing Feature: (+ zidovudine) → lipodystrophy; (+ lamivudine, didanosine) → peripheral neuropathy
Drug: Didanosine | Distinguishing Feature: Dose-dependent pancreatitis; (+ lamivudine, stavudine) → peripheral neuropathy
Drug: Abacavir | Distinguishing Feature: Hypersensitivity linked to HLA-B*57:01 (delayed type IV reaction)
Drug: Emtricitabine | Distinguishing Feature: Hyperpigmentation of palms/soles

children.label: NNRTIs — Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors
children: MOA → no phosphorylation needed; direct binding → allosteric inhibition of reverse transcriptase → halts DNA polymerase
AE (class) → variable CYP450 effects; Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Nevirapine → liver failure can occur within 6 weeks of starting therapy
Efavirenz → CNS AE (dizziness, drowsiness, headache, psychosis), insomnia/nightmares; teratogenic
Delavirdine → contraindicated in pregnancy

children.label: Protease Inhibitors
children: Suffix → "-navir"; not phosphorylated
MOA → inhibit protease → immature, non-infectious virion; POL gene codes HIV enzymes
Never used as monotherapy
AE (class) → hyperglycemia/insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, lipodystrophy
Indinavir → nephrolithiasis (prevent with adequate hydration)
Ritonavir → strongest CYP450 inhibitor → "boosts" concentrations of other protease inhibitors

children.label: Entry, Fusion & Integrase Inhibitors
children: Maraviroc (entry) → binds CCR5 (must determine viral tropism first)
Enfuvirtide (fusion) → binds gp41 → blocks fusion
Raltegravir (integrase) → binds/inhibits viral integrase → blocks DNA integration; AE → rhabdomyolysis

children.label: Key Drug Interaction
children: Rifampin → activates CYP450 → ↓ concentration of protease inhibitors

children.label: Overview
children: Immunomodulatory cytokines released by virus-infected cells; interleukins upregulate interferon synthesis.

Type: Interferon-α | Key Uses / Notes: Hep B & C; hairy cell leukemia; malignant melanoma; Kaposi sarcoma (HIV); condyloma acuminata (HPV); renal cell carcinoma. / AE → flu-like syndrome, fatigue, retinopathy, confusion; myelosuppression (+ zidovudine); lupus
Type: Interferon-β | Key Uses / Notes: Multiple sclerosis (MS)
Type: Interferon-γ | Key Uses / Notes: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)

children.label: Overview
children: Identify HCV genotype before treatment; assess liver fibrosis first
SVR (sustained virologic response) = undetectable HCV RNA by PCR 6 months after stopping treatment
Traditional regimen → weekly pegylated interferon-α + daily ribavirin

children.label: Ribavirin
children: Guanosine nucleoside analog; phosphorylated 3× by cellular enzymes → active form
AE → dose-dependent hemolytic anemia; teratogenic
Also classically used for RSV

children.label: Sofosbuvir
children: Nucleoside analog → inhibits NS5B RNA polymerase
AE → fatigue, nausea

children.label: Simeprevir
children: Protease inhibitor (NS3/4 protease)
AE → phototoxicity, rash; CYP450 inhibitor

children.label: Acyclovir & Valacyclovir (HSV, VZV)
children: MOA → guanosine analog → activated by viral thymidine kinase → monophosphate → cellular kinases → triphosphate → incorporates into DNA → halts synthesis
Resistance → absent thymidine kinase
Valacyclovir → prodrug, improved oral bioavailability; daily use = suppressive therapy for recurrent outbreaks
IV acyclovir → serious HSV/VZV infections, HSV encephalitis, neonatal infection
VZV → famciclovir/valacyclovir preferred over acyclovir (superior activity, less frequent dosing); most effective within 3 days of shingles onset
Prophylaxis → immunocompromised patients; pregnant women with recurrent genital herpes; organ transplant recipients
AE → interstitial nephritis/crystalline nephropathy (IV; prevent with hydration); uncommon CNS effects (delirium, confusion, vertigo, hallucinations)

children.label: Ganciclovir & Valganciclovir (CMV)
children: MOA → guanosine analog → activated by viral UL97 kinase → monophosphate → cellular kinase → triphosphate → incorporates into viral DNA → halts DNA polymerase
Uses → organ transplant prophylaxis; CMV retinitis (typically CD4 <50)
Valganciclovir → prodrug, better oral bioavailability; used in high-risk solid organ/bone marrow transplant recipients
AE → bone marrow suppression (additive with zidovudine)

children.label: Foscarnet & Cidofovir
children: MOA → do NOT require viral kinase phosphorylation → active against acyclovir/ganciclovir-resistant HSV, CMV, VZV; directly inhibit viral DNA polymerase
Foscarnet AE → renal insufficiency, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, seizures
Cidofovir AE → nephrotoxicity → proteinuria, azotemia, metabolic acidosis
Probenecid → blocks tubular secretion of cidofovir → ↓ toxicity (also ↑ plasma levels of penicillins, methotrexate, NSAIDs)

children.label: Overview
children: Nicotinic ACh receptors → ligand-gated ion channels → autonomic ganglia, skeletal muscle motor end plates, adrenal medulla
Muscarinic ACh receptors (M1, M2, M3) → GPCRs
Receptor: M1 | G-protein: Gq | Location: Nerves / CNS | Effect: ↑ IP3-DAG → ↑ intracellular Ca2+
Receptor: M2 | G-protein: Gi | Location: Atria, SA/AV node (not ventricles) | Effect: ↓ cAMP
Receptor: M3 | G-protein: Gq | Location: Glands, smooth muscle (vasculature, bladder, GI, eye) | Effect: ↑ IP3-DAG → ↑ Ca2+; vascular → NO release → ↑ cGMP → vasodilation
Atherosclerosis → endothelial damage → direct muscarinic activation → loses NO pathway → vasoconstriction
Net systemic effect of muscarinic agonists → ↓ BP (high doses can act on other M receptors)

children.label: Direct Muscarinic/Nicotinic Agonists
children: Bethanechol → ↑ gut motility/secretion → non-obstructive GI dysmotility (post-op/neurogenic ileus); urinary retention (neurogenic bladder)
Pilocarpine → ↑ salivation (Sjögren's, radiation-induced dry mouth); contracts ciliary muscle → ↑ aqueous outflow (glaucoma); miosis → useful in acute angle-closure glaucoma
Carbachol → muscarinic + nicotinic agonist → miosis → acute angle-closure glaucoma
Methacholine → bronchial challenge test (asthma diagnosis); can exacerbate asthma/COPD
All cholinomimetics → can cause peptic ulcers
Varenicline → nicotinic receptor partial agonist → smoking cessation

children.label: Overview
children: MOA → inhibit AChE (reversibly or irreversibly) → ↑ ACh at synapse (both muscarinic + nicotinic effects)
Suffix → "-stigmine"
↑ ACh at NMJ (nicotinic) → ↑ strength of contraction

children.label: Myasthenia Gravis (MG)
children: MG → autoantibodies vs nicotinic ACh receptors at NMJ → progressive weakness, ptosis, diplopia
Pyridostigmine → long-term MG treatment
Neostigmine → MG treatment
Edrophonium → transiently reverses MG symptoms → Tension Test: positive (improves) = undertreated MG; negative (no change) = cholinergic crisis
Pyridostigmine, neostigmine, edrophonium → quaternary amines → do NOT cross CNS (edrophonium effect lasts only 5–15 min)

children.label: NMJ Blockade
children: Non-depolarizing blockers (tubocurarine, pancuronium, cisatracurium) → competitive nicotinic antagonists at NMJ; reversed by neostigmine
Succinylcholine → depolarizing nicotinic agonist → sustained depolarization → unresponsive muscle; Phase 1 block is irreversible — AChE inhibitors worsen (potentiate) it
AChE inhibitors → also treat urinary retention (muscarinic activation)

children.label: Anticholinergic Overdose & Organophosphate Toxicity
children: Physostigmine → crosses CNS → reverses atropine/anticholinergic overdose (peripheral + central)
Anticholinergic toxidrome → "mad as a hatter, hot as a hare, blind as a bat" (also from belladonna/jimson weed ingestion)
Organophosphates (parathion, malathion, echothiopate; nerve agents, herbicides) → irreversible AChE inhibitors, cross CNS
Muscarinic toxicity — "DUMBBELSS": diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, lacrimation, salivation, sweating
Nicotinic toxicity → flaccid paralysis (NMJ over-stimulation)
Pralidoxime → regenerates AChE (hydrolyzes organophosphate bond) → reverses muscarinic + nicotinic toxicity, including flaccid paralysis; peripheral only
Atropine → reverses peripheral + central muscarinic toxicity only (no nicotinic effect)
Aging → organophosphate-AChE complex becomes irreversibly bound over time → pralidoxime ineffective after aging

children.label: Alzheimer's Disease (CNS-Penetrating AChE Inhibitors)
children: Galantamine, Rivastigmine, Donepezil → cross CNS → treat Alzheimer's disease

children.label: Overview
children: MOA → reversible, competitive block of muscarinic receptors ("anti-DUMBBELSS" — opposite of cholinergic toxicity)
Atropine → prototype; natural sources: belladonna (deadly nightshade), jimson weed

children.label: Eye & CNS
children: Cause mydriasis (pupil dilation) + cycloplegia (loss of near-vision accommodation)
Scopolamine → crosses BBB, blocks central M1 → motion sickness (give before symptom onset); transdermal patch

children.label: Cardiac
children: Block M2 at SA/AV node → ↑ HR, ↑ AV conduction
Atropine → treats bradycardia and heart block (AV block)

children.label: Respiratory
children: Ipratropium, Tiotropium → inhaled M3 antagonists → bronchodilation, ↓ secretions → COPD
Tiotropium → slower dissociation from M3 → longer duration of action

children.label: Genitourinary
children: Oxybutynin → relieves bladder spasm post-urologic surgery
Tolterodine → adult urinary incontinence
Both → M3 antagonism → relax bladder/ureter smooth muscle

children.label: CNS / Movement Disorders
children: M1 receptors → CNS; excess M1 activity → cogwheel rigidity in Parkinson's disease
Benztropine, Trihexyphenidyl → central M1 antagonists → treat Parkinsonian tremor/rigidity AND antipsychotic-induced extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism)

children.label: Adverse Effects (Anticholinergic Toxidrome)
children: ↑ HR; ↓ sweating → hyperthermia; ↓ salivation/lacrimation → dry mouth/eyes
Mydriasis/cycloplegia → blurred vision; mydriasis → ↓ aqueous outflow → acute angle-closure glaucoma
Crosses BBB → central M1 block → sedation, agitation, hallucination, coma (especially elderly)

children.label: Overview
children: Receptor: α1 | G-protein: Gq | Key Effects: Arterial + venous constriction → ↑ MAP, ↑ venous return; mydriasis; urethral/prostatic contraction → urinary retention
Receptor: α2 | G-protein: Gi | Key Effects: Presynaptic → ↓ NT release (central sympatholytic); ↓ insulin release; ↓ lipolysis; ↓ aqueous humor production
Receptor: β1 | G-protein: Gs | Key Effects: ↑ HR, ↑ contractility, ↑ CO; ↑ renin release (JGA)

Receptor: β2 | G-protein: Gs | Key Effects: Bronchodilation; coronary/skeletal vasodilation → ↓ SVR, ↓ diastolic BP; ↑ lipolysis; ↑ hepatic gluconeogenesis; ↑ insulin release (→ possible hypokalemia); ↑ aqueous humor production
Brimonidine → α2 agonist → ↓ aqueous humor production → treats open-angle glaucoma

children.label: Overview
children: Drug: Phenylephrine | Receptor Profile: α1 only | Key Effects / Uses: Nasal decongestant; mydriasis; ↑ MAP/systolic/diastolic BP; reflex bradycardia (baroreceptor response)
Drug: Norepinephrine | Receptor Profile: α1 > β1 | Key Effects / Uses: ↑ MAP, systolic & diastolic BP; reflex bradycardia; ↑ contractility (β1) → ↑ pulse pressure; used in septic/distributive shock

Drug: Epinephrine | Receptor Profile: β > α (dose-dependent) | Key Effects / Uses: Low dose: β effects → bronchodilation, ↓ diastolic BP, ↑ HR/contractility. High dose: α1 → vasoconstriction, ↑ SVR. Net ↑ MAP, ↑ pulse pressure. Drug of choice → anaphylaxis
Drug: Dobutamine | Receptor Profile: β1 >> β2 | Key Effects / Uses: ↑ HR, contractility, CO → refractory/cardiogenic heart failure; ↑ pulse pressure; used for cardiac stress testing
Drug: Isoproterenol | Receptor Profile: β1 = β2 | Key Effects / Uses: ↑ HR & contractility (β1); vasodilation → ↓ SVR, ↓ diastolic BP, ↓ MAP (β2); ↑ pulse pressure
Drug: Terbutaline, Ritodrine | Receptor Profile: β2 | Key Effects / Uses: Uterine relaxation → tocolysis (prevent premature labor)
Drug: Albuterol, Formoterol, Salmeterol | Receptor Profile: β2 | Key Effects / Uses: "-terol" suffix → bronchodilators

children.label: Catecholamine Synthesis, Storage & Reuptake
children: Tyrosine → (rate-limiting; blocked by Metyrosine) → L-DOPA → Dopamine → (dopamine β-hydroxylase, in vesicle) → Norepinephrine
VMAT → packages catecholamines into presynaptic vesicles
NET → reuptake of NE (+ dopamine); DAT → reuptake of dopamine — both targeted by antidepressants and cocaine

children.label: Cocaine
children: MOA → inhibits NET (peripheral) → sympathetic stimulation (HTN, tachycardia, mydriasis); inhibits DAT (central) → ↑ CNS dopamine → arousal, addiction, seizures
Complications → nasal mucosal atrophy/septal perforation (vasoconstriction); coronary vasospasm → angina/myocardial ischemia
Avoid beta-blockers in cocaine toxicity → unopposed α1 stimulation → severe HTN

children.label: Other Reuptake/Storage Agents & Stimulants
children: Atomoxetine → NET inhibitor → treats ADHD
Reserpine, Tetrabenazine → inhibit VMAT → deplete NT stores → AE: depression
Amphetamines → displace NE/dopamine into synapse → treat ADHD; suppress appetite
Methylphenidate → amphetamine derivative → ADHD
Modafinil → stimulant → narcolepsy; suppresses appetite

children.label: Dopamine — Dose-Dependent Receptor Activation
children: Dose: Low | Receptor: D1 (Gs) | Effect: ↑ renal blood flow, GFR, Na+ excretion
Dose: Medium | Receptor: β1 | Effect: ↑ cardiac contractility/output
Dose: High | Receptor: α1 | Effect: Vasoconstriction (pressor effect)
Use → pressor in heart failure or shock refractory to norepinephrine
D2 receptors → Gi-coupled; found in CNS

children.label: Alpha-2 Agonists (Central Sympatholytics)
children: Drug: Clonidine | Distinguishing Use: HTN (incl. hypertensive urgency); ADHD; Tourette's syndrome
Drug: Methyldopa | Distinguishing Use: HTN — especially gestational HTN; AE: lupus-like syndrome
Drug: Tizanidine | Distinguishing Use: Central-acting skeletal muscle relaxant

children.label: Alpha Antagonists
children: Phentolamine → reversible, non-selective α1/α2 antagonist → vasodilation; used for cocaine toxicity, MAOI + tyramine hypertensive crisis, pheochromocytoma (peri-/intra-operative)
Phenoxybenzamine → irreversible, non-selective α1/α2 antagonist → given days in advance of pheochromocytoma surgery
Pheochromocytoma → catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumor → headache, HTN, palpitations, sweating; alpha-blockade before beta-blockade
MAOIs + tyramine (wine, aged cheese) → prevents tyramine metabolism → hypertensive crisis → treat with alpha blockers
α1-selective antagonists — "-osin" (prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin) → vasodilation
Terazosin → BPH (relaxes prostatic/urethral smooth muscle); Prazosin → also used for PTSD
AE (alpha blockers) → orthostatic hypotension → reflex tachycardia
Mirtazapine → atypical antidepressant; α2 antagonist (+ other receptors) → ↑ serotonin release → treats depression

children.label: Overview
children: Suffix → "-lol"
MOA → antagonize β1 → ↓ contractility, ↓ HR, suppress SA/AV node conduction (risk: bradycardia, heart block)
↓ myocardial O2 demand → treats chronic stable angina
↓ renin release (β1 at JGA)

children.label: Selectivity
children: Cardioselective (β1): atenolol, betaxolol, esmolol, acebutolol, metoprolol → preferred in acute MI/ACS, chronic heart failure (↓ tachycardia/catecholamine burden)
Nonselective + α1 blockade: Carvedilol (heart failure); Labetalol → HTN in pregnancy, IV for hypertensive emergency
Partial agonists — Pindolol (nonselective), Acebutolol (β1-selective) → avoid in heart failure/post-MI

children.label: Clinical Uses
children: Post-MI / chronic HF → ↓ mortality (protect heart from catecholamine-induced remodeling)
HTN (especially post-MI); IV use → acute aortic dissection
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM)
Migraine prophylaxis (episodic); essential tremor; antiarrhythmic properties
Thyroid storm — "3 P's": Propranolol, Prednisone, Propylthiouracil
Topical nonselective (Timolol) → glaucoma (↓ aqueous humor production, ciliary epithelium β2 block)

children.label: Adverse Effects & Toxicity
children: Nonselective agents → can exacerbate asthma/COPD (β2 blockade → bronchoconstriction)
Impotence in men
Toxicity treatment → Glucagon (bypasses beta receptor to stimulate the heart)

children.label: Digoxin
children: MOA → inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na+ → ↑ Ca2+ influx via Na+/Ca2+ exchanger → ↑ contractility (positive inotrope)
Also → direct vagal stimulation → AV nodal inhibition → treats atrial arrhythmias (rate control)
Uses → chronic systolic heart failure (symptom relief only — does NOT ↓ mortality); AFib rate control (not first-line)
Toxicity risk factors → hypokalemia (exacerbates toxicity — e.g., from loop diuretics/diarrhea/vomiting); renal insufficiency (↓ clearance, long half-life); drugs that ↓ renal clearance
AE → hyperkalemia (acute toxicity); various arrhythmias; scooped/concave ST segments on EKG (chronic use); bradycardia; heart block
AE → GI: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain; xanthopsia (yellow vision)
Contraindication → SA node heart block; use caution with beta blockers
Toxicity treatment → digoxin immune Fab

children.label: Milrinone
children: MOA → inhibits phosphodiesterase → ↓ cAMP breakdown → ↑ contractility; also causes arterial dilation
Uses → heart failure — watch for hypotension

children.label: Nesiritide
children: MOA → BNP analog → ↑ cGMP → arteriolar + venous dilation → ↓ afterload and preload
Also causes natriuresis

children.label: Overview
children: MOA → metabolized → releases nitric oxide → ↑ cGMP in vascular smooth muscle → myosin light chain dephosphorylation → relaxation
Effect → primarily venodilation (↑ venous capacitance); some large-artery dilation; minimal arteriolar effect
Hemodynamics → ↓ preload, ↓ venous return/filling → ↓ wall stress → ↓ myocardial O2 demand
Uses → chronic stable angina; Prinzmetal angina; acute coronary syndrome; IV → hypertensive emergency; acute pulmonary edema
Sublingual → avoids first-pass metabolism (acute relief); Oral (isosorbide mono-/dinitrate) → longer duration, larger doses needed (first-pass metabolism)
Contraindications → right-sided MI (preload-dependent — use IV fluids instead); HOCM; PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) — avoid within 24 hours (severe hypotension)
AE → hypotension → reflex tachycardia (baroreceptor-mediated; beta blockers prevent this); throbbing headache, flushing; methemoglobinemia
Tolerance → prevent with daily nitrate-free interval; "Monday disease" — industrial workers lose tolerance over the weekend → headache/dizziness on Monday re-exposure

children.label: Lipoprotein Pathway (Overview)
children: Chylomicrons (intestine) → carry dietary triglycerides (main component) + cholesterol esters; surface ApoB-48, A, C, E; ApoE → hepatic uptake of remnants (via LDL receptor)
LPL → hydrolyzes chylomicron/VLDL triglycerides → free fatty acids (energy for heart/muscle, or re-esterified/stored in adipose)
HMG-CoA reductase → synthesizes cholesterol in liver (1st intermediate: mevalonic acid)
VLDL (liver) → carries triglycerides (~60%) to periphery; ApoB100 marks "bad cholesterol" (LDL & VLDL); LPL hydrolysis → loses triglycerides → becomes LDL
LDL → cholesterol-ester core; delivers cholesterol to peripheral LDL receptors; cleared by hepatic LDL receptor (ApoB100-mediated)

HDL (liver/intestine) → extracts cholesterol from peripheral membranes; LCAT esterifies free cholesterol; transfers esters to LDL/VLDL, or delivers directly to liver via scavenger receptor (SR-B1) — reverse cholesterol transport
Bile acids → liver converts cholesterol → bile acids → secreted in bile → 95% reabsorbed in terminal ileum (enterohepatic circulation)

children.label: Statins — Simvastatin, Atorvastatin, Rosuvastatin
children: MOA → inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↓ cholesterol synthesis → ↑ LDL receptor expression on hepatocytes → ↑ LDL clearance
Effect → ↓ LDL 30–60% (most potent); mild ↓ triglycerides; mild ↑ HDL
Uses → most effective for preventing CV events; only lipid drug proven to ↓ atherosclerotic CV disease risk; started in MI/ACS; ↓ CV events/mortality in high-risk diabetics, PAD, prior TIA/stroke
AE → teratogenic; myopathy (weeks–months after starting; proximal weakness, ↑ CK); mild reversible ↑ LFTs
Metabolism → all except pravastatin are metabolized via CYP450 → ↑ myopathy risk with interacting drugs

children.label: Bile Acid Resins — Cholestyramine, Colestipol, Colesevelam
children: MOA → bind bile acids in gut → block enterohepatic recycling → ↑ new bile acid synthesis (depletes hepatic cholesterol) → ↑ LDL receptor upregulation → ↑ LDL clearance
Uses → primary hypercholesterolemia

AE → ↑ triglycerides/VLDL (avoid if TG already high); gallstones; constipation/bloating (avoid in diverticulitis/bowel disease); impairs fat-soluble vitamin absorption (A, D, E, K); ↓ statin absorption (space 4 hours apart)

children.label: Ezetimibe
children: MOA → blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption → ↓ hepatic cholesterol delivery → ↑ LDL receptor upregulation → ↑ LDL clearance
Uses → adjunct to statin therapy
AE → diarrhea/steatorrhea; ↑ LFTs — does NOT cause gallstones or hypertriglyceridemia

children.label: PCSK9 Inhibitors — Evolocumab
children: MOA → antibody binds PCSK9 → prevents LDL receptor degradation → ↑ LDL receptor density → ↑ LDL clearance

children.label: Fibrates — Gemfibrozil, Fenofibrate
children: MOA → activate PPAR-alpha → ↑ LPL activity
Effect → ↓ triglycerides 35–50% (main effect); mild ↓ LDL; mild ↑ HDL (activates ApoA-I/A-II)
AE → ↑ myopathy risk when combined with statins; gallstones

children.label: Niacin (Vitamin B3)
children: Effect → most effective for ↑ HDL (~30%); ↓ triglycerides/VLDL (↓ hepatic secretion); mild ↓ LDL
AE → cutaneous flushing/warmth (prostaglandin-mediated — prevent with NSAIDs/aspirin); hyperglycemia; hyperuricemia (may precipitate gout); ↑ LFTs → hepatotoxicity (monitor)

children.label: Fish Oil (Omega-3 Fatty Acids)
children: Effect → ↓ triglycerides (↓ VLDL and ApoB production)
Drug: Statins | LDL: ↓↓↓ 30–60% | HDL: ↑ mild | TG: ↓ mild | Key Note: Best CV mortality benefit; myopathy, ↑CK
Drug: Bile acid resins | LDL: ↓ | HDL: — | TG: ↑ | Key Note: GI upset, gallstones, ↓ fat-soluble vitamins
Drug: Ezetimibe | LDL: ↓ | HDL: — | TG: — | Key Note: No gallstones/↑TG; adjunct to statin
Drug: PCSK9i (evolocumab) | LDL: ↓↓ | HDL: — | TG: — | Key Note: Antibody; prevents LDL-receptor degradation
Drug: Fibrates | LDL: ↓ mild | HDL: ↑ mild | TG: ↓↓ 35–50% | Key Note: Gallstones; ↑ myopathy risk with statins
Drug: Niacin | LDL: ↓ mild | HDL: ↑↑↑ ~30% | TG: ↓ | Key Note: Flushing, hepatotoxic, hyperglycemia/uricemia
Drug: Fish oil | LDL: — | HDL: — | TG: ↓ | Key Note: —

children.label: Overview
children: Target → voltage-gated L-type Ca2+ channels
Dihydropyridines ("-dipine": nifedipine, amlodipine, nicardipine) → block L-type channels in smooth muscle → vasodilation
Non-dihydropyridines — verapamil (minimal vasodilation), diltiazem (some vasodilation) → block L-type channels in cardiac muscle → ↓ contractility, ↓ SA/AV node activity → bradycardia

children.label: Uses
children: HTN → long-acting dihydropyridines; IV dihydropyridines (clevidipine, nicardipine) → hypertensive emergency; nifedipine → HTN in pregnancy/postpartum
Stable angina → dihydropyridines: coronary vasodilation → ↑ coronary blood flow, ↓ afterload → ↓ O2 demand; non-dihydropyridines: ↓ O2 demand via negative inotropy/chronotropy + ↓ BP
Prinzmetal angina (coronary vasospasm — rest/nocturnal episodes)
Raynaud's syndrome → nifedipine, amlodipine
Subarachnoid hemorrhage (berry aneurysm, associated with polycystic kidney disease) → nimodipine → prevents cerebral vasospasm
Migraine prophylaxis → verapamil
Non-dihydropyridines → also antiarrhythmic (AFib/flutter — see Class IV, Section VI)

children.label: Adverse Effects
children: Dihydropyridines → lightheadedness, headache, flushing; peripheral edema (precapillary arteriolar dilation → ↑ capillary hydrostatic pressure); reflex tachycardia (esp. nifedipine — short-acting form can exacerbate ischemia; avoid in unstable angina/MI)
Verapamil → constipation, gingival hyperplasia
Verapamil/diltiazem → relatively contraindicated in heart block; + beta blocker → risk of excessive AV block
CCBs → can worsen heart failure (hypotension, reflex sympathetic activation)

children.label: Primary (Essential) Hypertension
children: Use 2 agents if BP is >20/10 mmHg above goal
First-line → thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone), long-acting CCBs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs
Black and elderly patients → respond well to CCBs or thiazides
ACE inhibitors → first-line for HTN with heart failure, MI, or diabetes

children.label: Hypertensive Emergency
children: Definition → SBP >180 or DBP >120 + end-organ damage (blurry vision, lung crackles, headache)
Caution → many agents are potent vasodilators → reflex tachycardia, rebound hypotension, Na+/fluid retention (↑ renin)
Drug: Esmolol, Metoprolol (IV) | MOA: β1 antagonist | Key Notes: Acute BP control
Drug: Labetalol | MOA: α + β antagonist | Key Notes: Combined effect useful IV
Drug: Nicardipine, Clevidipine | MOA: Dihydropyridine CCB | Key Notes: Arteriolar dilation

Drug: Hydralazine | MOA: Direct arteriolar vasodilator | Key Notes: Safe in pregnancy; reflex tachycardia (pair with beta blocker); drug-induced lupus; + nitrate → mortality benefit in HF (LV systolic dysfunction)
Drug: Nitroprusside | MOA: NO-mediated arteriolar + venous dilation | Key Notes: Cyanide poisoning risk
Drug: Fenoldopam | MOA: Selective D1 agonist (↑ cAMP); no α/β effect | Key Notes: Coronary + renal vasodilation; natriuretic (↑ Na+/H2O excretion)

children.label: Overview
children: Myocyte AP: Phase 0 upstroke → Na+; Phase 2 plateau → Ca2+; Phase 3 repolarization → K+. Pacemaker cells (SA/AV node): Phase 4 → Na+ ("funny current") + other ions; upstroke → Ca2+; repolarization → K+.
Class: I | Target: Na+ channels | Main Effect: ↓ phase 0 slope → slows conduction | Example Drugs: Quinidine/procainamide/disopyramide (IA); lidocaine/mexiletine (IB); flecainide/propafenone (IC)
Class: II | Target: β receptors (↓ cAMP) | Main Effect: ↓ SA/AV pacemaker activity | Example Drugs: Metoprolol, esmolol
Class: III | Target: K+ channels | Main Effect: ↑ refractory period (↑ AP duration) | Example Drugs: Amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide
Class: IV | Target: Ca2+ channels (non-DHP) | Main Effect: ↓ SA/AV conduction | Example Drugs: Verapamil, diltiazem

children.label: Class I — Na+ Channel Blockers
children: Bind preferentially to open/inactivated channels → "use-dependence" (greater effect at higher HR)
Act only on Na+-dependent tissue (no effect at SA/AV nodes); widen QRS (more pronounced at higher HR)
Binding affinity: IC > IA > IB

Class: IA | Drugs: Quinidine, Procainamide, Disopyramide | Na+ Affinity / AP Effect: Intermediate affinity; ↑ AP duration (also blocks K+) → prolonged refractory period → QT prolongation → risk of torsades | Uses / Key Notes: SVT & VT, WPW syndrome. Quinidine → cinchonism, thrombocytopenia. Procainamide → lupus-like syndrome (↑ ANA). Disopyramide → ↓ contractility (worsens HF)

Class: IB | Drugs: Lidocaine, Mexiletine (phenytoin has some IB activity) | Na+ Affinity / AP Effect: Low affinity; ↓ AP duration → shortened refractory period (no torsades risk) | Uses / Key Notes: Ventricular arrhythmias, especially post-MI/ischemic tissue (preferential binding in depolarized tissue). AE: neuro effects (paresthesia, tremor, convulsions)

Class: IC | Drugs: Flecainide, Propafenone | Na+ Affinity / AP Effect: Strong affinity; no change in AP duration; marked QRS widening, prolongs AV nodal ERP | Uses / Key Notes: SVT (AFib/flutter) & VT — restore/maintain sinus rhythm. Contraindicated in structural/ischemic heart disease (proarrhythmic)

children.label: Class II — Beta Blockers
children: MOA → block sympathetic input to SA/AV nodes → ↓ cAMP → ↓ Ca2+ channel opening → ↓ pacemaker AP upstroke; prolongs phase 4 → ↓ pacemaker activity, ↑ conduction time/refractory period; ↓ AV conduction
Uses → SVT (AFib with RVR — rate control only, does not restore sinus rhythm); IV esmolol for acute SVT
AE → heart block → prolonged PR interval

children.label: Class III — K+ Channel Blockers
children: Drugs → Sotalol (also a beta blocker), Dofetilide, Ibutilide ("-tilide" suffix), Amiodarone (shares properties of Class I, II, III, and IV)
MOA → block K+ channels → prolong phase 2/3 → ↑ refractory period
Uses → SVT and VT; AFib/flutter — restore/maintain sinus rhythm
AE (class) → dose-related torsades (QT prolongation) — sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide

Amiodarone-specific AE → neuro (tremor, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, sleep disturbance); gray corneal deposits; thyroid dysfunction (hyper/hypo — check before & during use); pulmonary fibrosis (restrictive lung disease); can induce heart failure; hypersensitivity hepatitis (monitor LFTs); blue-gray skin discoloration; photodermatitis; CYP450 inhibitor

children.label: Class IV — Non-Dihydropyridine CCBs
children: Verapamil, Diltiazem → block L-type Ca2+ channels at SA/AV node (greater effect on frequently-firing tissue) → prolong phase 4 → ↓ pacemaker activity, ↑ conduction time/refractory period, ↓ AV conduction
Uses → SVT (AFib/flutter with RVR — rate control)
AE → prolonged PR interval; heart block (caution combining with digoxin or other AV-nodal blocking drugs)

children.label: Other Antiarrhythmic Agents
children: Digoxin → vagal stimulation → AV nodal inhibition → rate control in AFib/flutter (not first-line)
Magnesium → treats torsades de pointes
Hyperkalemia → peaked T waves, shortened QT (arrhythmogenic); Hypokalemia → U waves, muscle weakness, glucose abnormalities (arrhythmogenic)
Adenosine → activates inhibitory A1 receptors (SA/AV node, myocardium) → ↑ K+ efflux (hyperpolarization) + ↓ Ca2+ current → ↓ AV conduction, transient high-grade heart block (~10 sec)
Adenosine → first-line for acute PSVT; also causes coronary vasodilation (A2 receptors)
Adenosine AE → flushing, chest pain/dyspnea, sense of impending doom, hypotension, headache
Adenosine effect → blocked by methylxanthines (caffeine, theophylline)

children.label: Broad-Spectrum AEDs — Valproate, Topiramate, Lamotrigine, Levetiracetam
children: Uses → treat focal and generalized seizures, including juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
Many AEDs are metabolized by hepatic CYP450

children.label: Broad-Spectrum AEDs — Valproate, Topiramate, Lamotrigine, Levetiracetam › Valproate
children: MOA → ↑ Na+ channel inactivation; ↑ GABA levels in CNS
AE → GI distress (nausea, vomiting); ↑ appetite/weight gain; tremor; fatal hepatotoxicity; pancreatitis
Teratogenic → neural tube defects (spina bifida)
Also effective for absence seizures

children.label: Broad-Spectrum AEDs — Valproate, Topiramate, Lamotrigine, Levetiracetam › Topiramate
children: MOA → ↑ Na+ channel inactivation; allosteric GABA-A binding
AE → somnolence/fatigue; confusion/cognitive slowing; weight loss; acute angle-closure glaucoma; Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS/TEN); diplopia
Also used for migraine prophylaxis

children.label: Broad-Spectrum AEDs — Valproate, Topiramate, Lamotrigine, Levetiracetam › Lamotrigine
children: MOA → ↑ Na+ channel inactivation
Also effective for absence seizures

children.label: Broad-Spectrum AEDs — Valproate, Topiramate, Lamotrigine, Levetiracetam › Levetiracetam
children: AE → somnolence

children.label: Narrow-Spectrum AEDs — Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Gabapentin, Vigabatrin, Tiagabine
children: Uses → focal seizures (and generalized tonic-clonic)

children.label: Narrow-Spectrum AEDs — Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Gabapentin, Vigabatrin, Tiagabine › Carbamazepine
children: MOA → ↑ Na+ channel inactivation
Uses → 1st-line for trigeminal neuralgia
AE → ataxia, diplopia, SIADH, agranulocytosis, DRESS syndrome, SJS/TEN, drug-induced lupus
Induces CYP450
Teratogenic → neural tube defects

children.label: Narrow-Spectrum AEDs — Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Gabapentin, Vigabatrin, Tiagabine › Phenytoin
children: MOA → ↑ Na+ channel inactivation
AE → ataxia, diplopia, folate deficiency → megaloblastic anemia, gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, drug-induced lupus, DRESS, SJS/TEN, ↓ bone density
Teratogenic → cleft palate
Induces CYP450
Used for maintenance therapy after acute status epilepticus treatment

children.label: Narrow-Spectrum AEDs — Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Gabapentin, Vigabatrin, Tiagabine › Gabapentin
children: MOA → blocks voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
Uses → chronic/neuropathic pain, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, post-herpetic neuralgia (VZV reactivation)
AE → ataxia

children.label: Narrow-Spectrum AEDs — Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Gabapentin, Vigabatrin, Tiagabine › Vigabatrin & Tiagabine
children: Vigabatrin → irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase (↓ GABA degradation)
Tiagabine → inhibits GABA reuptake

children.label: Status Epilepticus
children: Acute → IV benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam); maintenance → phenytoin
Refractory seizures → IV phenobarbital

children.label: Absence Seizures
children: Presentation → sudden momentary lapse in awareness (staring, blinking, tonic jerks); 3 Hz spike-wave complexes on EEG
Treatment → ethosuximide (blocks T-type Ca2+ channels in thalamus); also valproate, lamotrigine
Ethosuximide AE → GI distress, lethargy/fatigue
Drug: Valproate | MOA: ↑Na+ inactivation, ↑GABA | Distinctive AE / Notes: Hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, neural tube defects
Drug: Topiramate | MOA: ↑Na+ inactivation, GABA-A binding | Distinctive AE / Notes: Weight loss, glaucoma, SJS
Drug: Lamotrigine | MOA: ↑Na+ inactivation | Distinctive AE / Notes: Also treats absence seizures
Drug: Levetiracetam | MOA: — | Distinctive AE / Notes: Somnolence
Drug: Carbamazepine | MOA: ↑Na+ inactivation | Distinctive AE / Notes: Agranulocytosis, SIADH; CYP450 inducer; 1st-line trigeminal neuralgia
Drug: Phenytoin | MOA: ↑Na+ inactivation | Distinctive AE / Notes: Gingival hyperplasia, megaloblastic anemia; CYP450 inducer
Drug: Gabapentin | MOA: ↓ Ca2+ channels | Distinctive AE / Notes: Neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, PHN
Drug: Ethosuximide | MOA: Blocks T-type Ca2+ (thalamus) | Distinctive AE / Notes: Absence seizures only

children.label: Overview
children: GABA-A receptor = Cl– channel. GABA (+ glycine) = major inhibitory CNS neurotransmitter. Barbiturates, benzodiazepines, and alcohol each bind separate allosteric sites on GABA-A.

children.label: Barbiturates
children: MOA → ↑ duration of GABA-A channel opening
Thiopental → IV induction of anesthesia; rapid onset/short duration (highly lipid-soluble); rapid redistribution to skeletal muscle/adipose → quick recovery
Phenobarbital (IV) → treats seizures, including refractory status epilepticus
Primidone → treats essential tremor (1st-line with propranolol)
AE → hypotension; cardiac/respiratory depression; severe CNS depression (coma) — avoid in elderly (long half-life, up to 100 hrs)
Chronic use → tolerance, physical dependence
Potent CYP450 inducers

children.label: Benzodiazepines
children: Suffix → "-pam" (diazepam, lorazepam, oxazepam); short-acting "-olam" (triazolam, alprazolam, midazolam)
MOA → ↑ frequency of GABA-A channel opening
Metabolized by liver; long-acting agents form active metabolites
Uses → alcohol withdrawal (long-acting: diazepam, chlordiazepoxide); status epilepticus; general anesthesia (muscle relaxation, amnesia); conscious sedation
Uses → insomnia (not 1st-line — dependence risk); parasomnias in children; spasticity (UMN disorders: MS, stroke, spinal cord trauma, tetanus); GAD & panic disorder (SSRIs/SNRIs 1st-line)
AE → tolerance (GABA-A downregulation); anterograde amnesia; elderly → ↑ sensitivity (somnolence, confusion, disorientation, central ataxia → falls)
Avoid with other CNS depressants (1st-gen antihistamines, alcohol, barbiturates, neuroleptics)
Addiction potential → more common with short-acting agents
Flumazenil (competitive BZD antagonist) → reverses benzo sedation (can precipitate seizures)

children.label: Benzodiazepines › Alcohol Withdrawal Timeline
children: 8–12 hours → insomnia, tremulousness, anxiety, autonomic instability
48–96 hours → delirium tremens (fever, disorientation, severe agitation)

children.label: Nonbenzodiazepine Hypnotics ("Z-drugs") — Zolpidem, Zaleplon, Eszopiclone
children: MOA → bind same allosteric site as benzodiazepines on GABA-A
Zaleplon/zolpidem → rapid onset, short duration, rapidly hepatically metabolized → sleep-onset insomnia
Eszopiclone → longest half-life → treats sleep-onset AND sleep-maintenance insomnia
AE → elderly ↑ sensitivity (cognitive impairment, delirium), central ataxia → falls; avoid with other CNS depressants
Less likely to cause tolerance, withdrawal, or dependence (vs. benzodiazepines)
Also reversed by flumazenil

children.label: Melatonin Receptor Agonists — Melatonin, Ramelteon
children: MT1/MT2 receptors (suprachiasmatic nucleus, hypothalamus) → maintain circadian rhythm
Ramelteon → MT1/MT2 agonist → treats insomnia; few side effects, safe in geriatric patients
Class: Barbiturates | Binding Site: Separate allosteric site | Effect on Cl– Channel: ↑ duration of opening | Distinguishing Feature: Long half-life, resp/cardiac depression, CYP450 inducer

Class: Benzodiazepines | Binding Site: Separate allosteric site | Effect on Cl– Channel: ↑ frequency of opening | Distinguishing Feature: Alcohol withdrawal, seizures, anterograde amnesia; reversed by flumazenil
Class: Z-drugs | Binding Site: Same site as benzodiazepines | Effect on Cl– Channel: (as benzo, shorter-acting) | Distinguishing Feature: Less tolerance/dependence; insomnia only
Class: Alcohol | Binding Site: Separate allosteric site | Effect on Cl– Channel: — | Distinguishing Feature: —

children.label: Overview
children: Pathophysiology → trigeminal nerve afferents in meninges activated → release CGRP, substance P, neurokinin A → meningeal vasodilation + protein extravasation
Triptans (sumatriptan) → 5-HT1B/5-HT1D agonists (meningeal vessels, trigeminal nerve, brainstem)
Triptan effects → vasoconstriction of cerebral/meningeal vessels; ↓ vasoactive peptide release from trigeminal nerve; inhibit brainstem pain pathways
Triptan uses → acute migraine treatment; acute cluster headache (with inhaled O2)
Triptan AE → coronary vasospasm — contraindicated in angina; known trigger of Prinzmetal angina
NSAIDs → acute migraine treatment
Prophylaxis → CCBs, beta blockers, valproic acid, topiramate, TCAs (amitriptyline)

children.label: Overview
children: Levodopa (L-DOPA) → crosses BBB → converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase (CNS AND periphery)
AE (peripheral conversion) → GI distress, cardiac arrhythmias, orthostatic hypotension
AE (CNS) → neuropsychiatric symptoms (anxiety, agitation, insomnia, confusion, hallucinations)

Chronic levodopa → wearing-off reaction (symptoms return at end of dose); on-off phenomenon (unpredictable, dose-independent); dyskinesias (choreoathetosis of face/distal extremities); therapeutic window narrows as disease progresses
Levodopa contraindicated in psychotic patients
Carbidopa → peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor → ↑ levodopa bioavailability, ↓ peripheral AE — but worsens neuropsychiatric AE
COMT inhibitors → block levodopa→3-OMD (periphery) and dopamine→3-MT (CNS) conversion → ↑ levodopa bioavailability / ↑ CNS dopamine
Entacapone → peripheral only. Tolcapone → peripheral AND central; AE → hepatic failure
Selegiline (selective MAO-B inhibitor) → ↑ CNS dopamine
Dopamine agonists → Ropinirole (D2), Pramipexole (D3) → initial Parkinson's treatment; also treat restless leg syndrome; AE → impulse control disorders (gambling, shopping, hypersexuality)
Amantadine → ↑ endogenous dopamine synthesis/release, ↓ reuptake → treats some motor symptoms
Trihexyphenidyl & Benztropine (antimuscarinics) → improve tremor and rigidity (no effect on bradykinesia)

children.label: Inhaled Anesthetics
children: N2O → gaseous; volatile agents (enflurane, isoflurane, halothane) → liquid at room temp, fluorinated
Low solubility (↓ blood:gas coefficient, e.g., N2O) → steep arterial tension curve → fast onset, fast recovery
High solubility (↑ blood:gas coefficient, e.g., halothane) → less steep curve → slow onset, longer duration
MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) → dose causing 50% of patients unresponsive to painful stimuli; 1/MAC = potency
AE → respiratory depression (↓ minute ventilation, hypercapnia); fluorinated agents → ↑ cerebral blood flow (↓ cerebrovascular resistance)
Halothane → hepatotoxic (massive hepatic necrosis)
Enflurane → nephrotoxic; can induce seizures

children.label: Malignant Hyperthermia
children: Skeletal muscle hypersensitivity to volatile anesthetics (also triggered by succinylcholine)
MOA → defective ryanodine receptor (RyR) in SR → excess Ca2+ release → excessive ATP-dependent reuptake → heat production → muscle damage (rhabdomyolysis)
Treatment → dantrolene (blocks ryanodine receptors)

children.label: IV Anesthetics
children: Benzodiazepines → conscious sedation for minor procedures (e.g., colonoscopy)
Drug: Propofol | MOA: ↑ GABA-A Cl– current | Key Feature: Induction + maintenance; vasodilation → hypotension
Drug: Etomidate | MOA: ↑ GABA-A Cl– current | Key Feature: Induction only; preserves cardiovascular stability
Drug: Ketamine | MOA: NMDA receptor antagonist | Key Feature: "Dissociative anesthesia"; ↑ BP/HR/CO; emergence reactions (vivid dreams, hallucinations)
Drug: Thiopental | MOA: Barbiturate (GABA-A) | Key Feature: Rapid onset/short duration (redistribution to muscle/fat); induction

children.label: Overview
children: μ-opioid receptor → mediates most clinical/adverse effects (analgesia, sedation, constipation, respiratory depression)
MOA → opens K+ channels, closes voltage-gated Ca2+ channels → ↓ presynaptic NT release (glutamate, ACh, NE, serotonin, substance P)
AE → CNS depression (sedation); respiratory depression; miosis; constipation; biliary colic (contracts biliary smooth muscle)
Tolerance develops to most effects — NOT to miosis or constipation
Chronic use → opioid-induced hyperalgesia
Withdrawal → rhinorrhea, lacrimation, yawning, hyperventilation, hyperthermia, muscle aches, vomiting, diarrhea, anxiety
Neonatal abstinence syndrome → diarrhea, sweating, sneezing, crying, tachypnea, irritability
Agent(s): Morphine, Fentanyl | Role: Full μ-agonists | Notes: Analgesia
Agent(s): Tramadol | Role: Weak μ-agonist | Notes: Also inhibits NE/serotonin reuptake; chronic pain
Agent(s): Loperamide, Diphenoxylate | Role: Antidiarrheal | Notes: Loperamide → ↑ colonic segmentation → ↓ stool transit
Agent(s): Codeine, Dextromethorphan | Role: Antitussive | Notes: Dextromethorphan → also NMDA antagonist
Agent(s): Methadone, Buprenorphine | Role: Long-acting (detox) | Notes: Attenuate withdrawal; buprenorphine = partial μ-agonist
Agent(s): Naloxone | Role: μ-antagonist | Notes: Reverses acute opioid toxicity; can precipitate withdrawal
Agent(s): Naltrexone | Role: μ-antagonist | Notes: Maintains abstinence (heroin); ↓ alcohol/nicotine cravings; aids weight loss

children.label: SSRIs — Fluoxetine, Paroxetine, Sertraline, Citalopram
children: MOA → inhibit presynaptic reuptake of serotonin (5-HT)
Uses → 1st-line for depression, GAD, panic disorder, PTSD; also OCD, bulimia, social anxiety disorder
Onset → 1–2 months to max effect (not for acute treatment)
AE → hyponatremia (SIADH); sexual dysfunction; weight gain; drowsiness; serotonin syndrome
Withdrawal → flu-like symptoms

children.label: SNRIs — Venlafaxine, Duloxetine
children: MOA → inhibit presynaptic reuptake of norepinephrine AND serotonin
Uses → same as SSRIs (1st-line depression, GAD, panic disorder, PTSD) plus diabetic neuropathy, chronic/neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia
Onset → 1–2 months
AE → hypertension; serotonin syndrome; flu-like withdrawal

children.label: TCAs — Imipramine, Desipramine, Clomipramine, Amitriptyline, Nortriptyline
children: MOA → inhibit presynaptic reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine
Uses → treatment-resistant depression (limited use — lethal in overdose); diabetic/neuropathic pain; migraine prophylaxis; clomipramine → OCD (SSRIs still 1st-line)
Secondary amines (nortriptyline, desipramine) → less cholinergic effect
AE (anticholinergic) → dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention
AE (antihistamine/α1) → sedation, ↑ appetite/weight gain (H1 block); orthostatic hypotension (α1 block)
Relatively contraindicated in elderly (anticholinergic + antihistamine effects)
AE (cardiac) → blocks fast Na+ channels → widened QRS, can induce torsades
AE → seizures; sexual dysfunction; serotonin syndrome
Overdose treatment → sodium bicarbonate (widened QRS, ventricular arrhythmia)

children.label: MAOIs — Tranylcypromine, Phenelzine, Isocarboxazid; Selegiline (MAO-B selective)
children: MAO-A → breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine
MOA → irreversible MAO inhibition
Uses → atypical depression; historically used, now last resort/treatment-resistant depression
Selegiline (selective MAO-B inhibitor) → ↑ CNS dopamine → used in Parkinson's disease
Dietary interaction → avoid tyramine-containing foods (normally broken down by MAO-A in gut) → excess tyramine acts as sympathomimetic → hypertensive crisis (HTN, blurry vision, diaphoresis)
Treatment of hypertensive crisis → phentolamine (α1/α2 blocker)
AE → serotonin syndrome — avoid combining with other serotonergic drugs (TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs)

children.label: Atypical Antidepressants › Bupropion
children: MOA → inhibits NET and DAT (norepinephrine + dopamine reuptake inhibitor)
CNS-activating; treats tobacco dependence
AE → seizures → contraindicated in bulimia and anorexia nervosa
Does NOT cause sexual dysfunction; less likely to cause weight gain

children.label: Atypical Antidepressants › Mirtazapine
children: MOA → blocks α2 receptors → ↑ presynaptic release of serotonin/NE; also blocks 5-HT2, 5-HT3, H1
Can be used as 1st-line (atypical antidepressant)
AE → sedation, weight gain; does NOT cause sexual dysfunction

children.label: Atypical Antidepressants › Trazodone
children: MOA → serotonin modulator — antagonizes 5-HT2 receptors + inhibits 5-HT reuptake; also blocks α1, H1
AE → priapism; orthostatic hypotension; sedation; sexual dysfunction; serotonin syndrome

children.label: Serotonin Syndrome
children: Presentation → hyperthermia, hypertension, neuromuscular hyperactivity (hyperreflexia, clonus)
Precipitated by → combining serotonergic drugs (SSRIs/SNRIs + TCAs or MAOIs)
Treatment → cyproheptadine (5-HT2 blocker)

Class: SSRIs | MOA: ↓ serotonin reuptake | Key Uses: 1st-line: depression, GAD, panic, PTSD; also OCD, bulimia, social anxiety | Key AE: Hyponatremia, sexual dysfunction, weight gain, serotonin syndrome
Class: SNRIs | MOA: ↓ NE + serotonin reuptake | Key Uses: Same as SSRIs + diabetic neuropathy, chronic pain, fibromyalgia | Key AE: HTN, serotonin syndrome

Class: TCAs | MOA: ↓ NE + serotonin reuptake | Key Uses: Treatment-resistant depression; neuropathic pain; migraine prophylaxis; clomipramine → OCD | Key AE: Anticholinergic; cardiotoxic (↑QRS → torsades); lethal in overdose
Class: MAOIs | MOA: Irreversible MAO inhibition | Key Uses: Atypical depression; last-resort; selegiline → Parkinson's | Key AE: Tyramine-induced HTN crisis; serotonin syndrome
Class: Bupropion | MOA: ↓ NE + dopamine reuptake | Key Uses: Atypical 1st-line; tobacco dependence; no sexual dysfunction | Key AE: Seizures (avoid in bulimia/anorexia)
Class: Mirtazapine | MOA: α2 antagonist; blocks 5-HT2/3, H1 | Key Uses: Atypical 1st-line | Key AE: Sedation, weight gain
Class: Trazodone | MOA: 5-HT2 antagonist + reuptake inhibition | Key Uses: — | Key AE: Priapism, orthostatic hypotension, sedation, serotonin syndrome

children.label: Overview
children: Lithium → treats bipolar disorder (acute mania AND maintenance); narrow therapeutic index
Lithium acute toxicity → GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea)
Lithium chronic toxicity → neurologic symptoms (tremor, ataxia)
Lithium AE → hypothyroidism (weight gain, dry skin, hair loss, constipation); nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Lithium levels ↑ with thiazide diuretics and NSAIDs (↓ GFR → ↓ clearance)
Lithium is teratogenic → Ebstein's anomaly (atrialization of right ventricle, associated with ASD and malformed tricuspid valve)
Valproate → bipolar disorder (acute mania AND maintenance)
Carbamazepine → bipolar disorder (acute mania AND maintenance)
Lamotrigine → bipolar disorder (maintenance only)
Antipsychotics (1st-gen e.g. haloperidol; 2nd-gen e.g. quetiapine) → treat acute mania

children.label: First-Generation (Typical) Antipsychotics — FGAs
children: Suffix → "-azine" (trifluoperazine, fluphenazine, chlorpromazine, thioridazine)
High potency → haloperidol, trifluoperazine, fluphenazine. Low potency → thioridazine, chlorpromazine
MOA → block D2 receptors in CNS
Uses → positive symptoms of schizophrenia; acute psychosis (e.g., bipolar); acute agitation/aggression; Tourette syndrome
Highly lipophilic → long half-life
AE (low potency > high potency) → anticholinergic (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention); orthostatic hypotension (α1 block); sedation (H1 block)
AE (high potency > low potency) → EPS, tardive dyskinesia, hyperprolactinemia (galactorrhea, amenorrhea, impotence), neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
Other AE → torsades de pointes; ↓ seizure threshold; chlorpromazine → corneal deposits; thioridazine → retinal deposits
NMS → "lead-pipe" rigidity, altered mental status, fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis

children.label: Second-Generation (Atypical) Antipsychotics — SGAs
children: Drugs → quetiapine, olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole, ziprasidone, clozapine
MOA → block D2 + 5-HT2A receptors
Uses → schizophrenia (positive AND negative symptoms); treatment-resistant depression (adjunct); OCD (risperidone, adjunct with SSRIs); Tourette syndrome (risperidone)
AE → sedation (H1 block), orthostatic hypotension (α1 block); lower muscarinic affinity than FGAs (fewer anticholinergic effects), though notable with clozapine
Metabolic AE (esp. olanzapine, clozapine) → weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia
Clozapine → agranulocytosis; myocarditis/cardiomyopathy; ↓ seizure threshold
EPS, hyperprolactinemia, NMS → FGA > SGA; risperidone → highest EPS risk among SGAs
Can also cause torsades de pointes
Onset: Minutes | Extrapyramidal Symptom (EPS): Acute dystonia
Onset: Days | Extrapyramidal Symptom (EPS): Akathisia
Onset: Weeks | Extrapyramidal Symptom (EPS): Drug-induced Parkinsonism

children.label: FGA vs SGA — Quick Comparison
children: Feature: Receptor blockade | FGA: D2 (+ M, H1, α1 — low potency agents) | SGA: D2 + 5-HT2A
Feature: Target symptoms | FGA: Positive only | SGA: Positive + negative
Feature: EPS / tardive dyskinesia | FGA: High potency agents (haloperidol etc.) | SGA: Lower risk (risperidone highest of SGAs)
Feature: Hyperprolactinemia | FGA: High potency agents | SGA: Less common
Feature: NMS risk | FGA: Higher | SGA: Lower
Feature: Metabolic effects | FGA: Less prominent | SGA: Olanzapine, clozapine → weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia
Feature: Notable unique AE | FGA: Chlorpromazine → corneal deposits; thioridazine → retinal deposits | SGA: Clozapine → agranulocytosis, myocarditis

children.label: Insulin Physiology & Secretion
children: Insulin = primary anabolic/storage hormone; made by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans
Glucose = most potent stimulus for insulin release (also sympathetic β2 activation)
MOA: Glucose ↑ATP in beta cell → ATP-dependent K+ channels close → depolarization → voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open → Ca2+ influx → insulin secretion
C-peptide is co-released with endogenous insulin (cleaved from proinsulin) → marker of endogenous insulin production
Insulin receptor = intracellular tyrosine kinase → phosphorylation cascade → inserts GLUT4 into cell membrane (muscle & adipose)

children.label: Insulin Physiology & Secretion › Actions of Insulin
children: Liver: ↑ glycogenesis, ↓ glycogenolysis
Muscle: ↑ glycogen storage, ↑ protein synthesis
Adipose: ↑ triglyceride storage
↓ Serum K+ (↑ Na+/K+ ATPase in skeletal muscle drives K+ into cells)

children.label: Insulin Physiology & Secretion › Insulin Preparations
children: Class: Rapid-acting | Agents: Lispro, Aspart, Glulisine | Onset / Duration: Rapid onset, short duration | Key Points: Do not form hexamers → fast absorption; controls postprandial spike

Class: Short / Intermediate | Agents: Regular, NPH | Onset / Duration: Delayed onset, intermediate duration (NPH more delayed) | Key Points: Form dimers/hexamers (slow breakdown); Regular = only insulin given IV
Class: Long-acting | Agents: Detemir, Glargine | Onset / Duration: Long duration — steady basal level | Key Points: Glargine has no peak

children.label: Insulin Physiology & Secretion › Clinical Pearls
children: DKA (vomiting, fatigue, polyuria) → treat with IV regular insulin (watch K+)
Hyperkalemia → treat with IV regular insulin + glucose
Insulin-induced hypoglycemia: tachycardia, palpitations, sweating, nausea → treat with glucagon

children.label: Oral / Injectable Agents — Type 2 Diabetes
children: Secretagogues below require functional beta cells for endogenous insulin release.

children.label: Oral / Injectable Agents — Type 2 Diabetes › Sulfonylureas & Meglitinides
children: MOA: bind/close ATP-dependent K+ channels on beta cells → depolarization → Ca2+ influx → endogenous insulin release (↑ C-peptide)
1st-gen ("-amide": tolbutamide, chlorpropamide): long duration, rarely used; chlorpropamide → disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol
2nd-gen ("-ride": glyburide, glimepiride): smaller doses, long duration; glipizide = shortest duration → lowest hypoglycemia risk
Meglitinides ("-glinide": repaglinide, nateglinide): same MOA, not sulfa drugs → safe with sulfa allergy
AE: hypoglycemia, weight gain

children.label: Oral / Injectable Agents — Type 2 Diabetes › GLP-1 Agonists & DPP-4 Inhibitors
children: GLP-1 agonists ("-tide": exenatide, liraglutide): directly activate GLP-1 receptor
DPP-4 inhibitors ("-gliptin": sitagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin): block GLP-1 breakdown → ↑ endogenous GLP-1
Effects: ↑ insulin release & satiety; ↓ glucagon release & gastric emptying
Do NOT cause hypoglycemia; ↑ endogenous insulin & C-peptide levels
AE: DPP-4i → ↑ URI / nasopharyngitis; GLP-1 agonists (exenatide) → pancreatitis (seek immediate care)

children.label: Oral / Injectable Agents — Type 2 Diabetes › Biguanides — Metformin (1st-line agent)
children: MOA: inhibits mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase + activates AMPK → ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↑ insulin sensitivity
AE: GI upset (most common — nausea, anorexia, vomiting, diarrhea); lactic acidosis (risk ↑ with renal insufficiency); modest weight loss

children.label: Oral / Injectable Agents — Type 2 Diabetes › Thiazolidinediones ("Glitazones") — rosiglitazone, pioglitazone
children: MOA: PPAR-γ ligand (muscle/fat/liver) → ↑ gene transcription → ↑ insulin sensitivity; ↑ adiponectin; ↑ GLUT4 in periphery
↑ adipocyte number/differentiation; ↑ TG storage & fatty acid oxidation → ↓ serum triglycerides
Onset: days to weeks
AE: weight gain; fluid retention/edema → can precipitate CHF; ↑ risk of atypical extremity fractures in women (↓ bone density)

children.label: Oral / Injectable Agents — Type 2 Diabetes › Other Agents
children: Amylin analog (pramlintide): ↓ glucagon, ↓ gastric emptying, ↓ appetite; controls postprandial spike; used in T1DM & T2DM; AE: hypoglycemia, GI upset

Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose, miglitol): inhibit brush-border alpha-glucosidase → delayed carb absorption; controls postprandial spike; AE: diarrhea, flatulence, abdominal pain (colonic fermentation)

SGLT2 inhibitors ("-flozin": canagliflozin, dapagliflozin — 2nd/3rd-line): inhibit SGLT2 in proximal convoluted tubule → glucosuria; AE: ↑ UTI, ↑ vaginal candidiasis, hypotension (osmotic diuresis); contraindicated in renal insufficiency

children.label: Antiemetics › Vomiting Pathway
children: Nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) = vomiting center (medulla); integrates GI, vestibular & area postrema input
GI tract → vagal afferents (CN X) → NTS; GI irritation (infection, chemo, distension) → mucosal serotonin release → activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents
Vestibular system → CN VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve) → NTS → mediates motion sickness / vertigo
Area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone): outside the BBB, in the 4th ventricle; responds to emetogens (e.g. chemo agents); contains D2 and NK1 receptors

children.label: Antiemetics › Antiemetic Drugs
children: Drug(s): Ondansetron | MOA / Target: 5-HT3 antagonist (vagal afferents) | Main Use: Chemo-induced & post-op vomiting | Key Adverse Effects: Constipation, headache/dizziness, QT prolongation → torsades, serotonin syndrome
Drug(s): Diphenhydramine, meclizine (1st-gen H1 blockers) | MOA / Target: H1 antagonist (vestibular, Gq) | Main Use: Vestibular nausea / motion sickness | Key Adverse Effects: —
Drug(s): Scopolamine | MOA / Target: M1 muscarinic antagonist (vestibular) | Main Use: Vestibular nausea / motion sickness | Key Adverse Effects: —

Drug(s): Metoclopramide | MOA / Target: D2 antagonist (area postrema) + upper-GI prokinetic | Main Use: Chemo-induced vomiting; diabetic gastroparesis; postsurgical delayed emptying | Key Adverse Effects: Diarrhea, drowsiness (elderly), depression, EPS, tardive dyskinesia, NMS, ↑prolactin, QT prolongation; CI: bowel obstruction
Drug(s): NK1 antagonists (e.g. aprepitant) | MOA / Target: Block NK1 receptor (area postrema; blocks substance P) | Main Use: Chemo-induced vomiting | Key Adverse Effects: —
Metoclopramide prokinetic effects: ↑ esophageal peristalsis, ↓ LES pressure, ↑ gastric emptying

children.label: Gastric Acid Secretion & Suppression
children: Parietal cells secrete acid via luminal H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) — exchanges 1 K+ for 1 H+
Histamine (from ECL cells) → H2 receptor (Gs → ↑cAMP) → ↑ H+/K+ ATPase → main driver of acid secretion
Gastrin (from G cells): major effect = stimulates ECL cells to release histamine; minor direct parietal cell effect
Vagal stimulation: directly stimulates parietal cell (M3) AND stimulates G cells to release gastrin (via GRP)

children.label: Gastric Acid Secretion & Suppression › H2 Blockers — "-tidine" (ranitidine, cimetidine, famotidine, nizatidine)
children: MOA: block H2 receptors → ↓ histamine-driven acid secretion
Use: GERD & duodenal ulcers (PPIs are 1st-line); best for nocturnal acid suppression; only modest effect on meal-stimulated acid (vagal pathway persists)
Cimetidine: inhibits CYP450; antiandrogenic → gynecomastia, impotence, ↑ prolactin

children.label: Gastric Acid Secretion & Suppression › PPIs — "-prazole" (omeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole)
children: MOA: irreversibly inhibit H+/K+ ATPase (final common pathway)
Use: GERD/ulcers (1st-line, faster relief); Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma); H. pylori (+ clarithromycin & amoxicillin/metronidazole)
AE: ↑ C. diff risk, ↑ respiratory infections, ↓ Ca2+/Mg2+/Fe2+ absorption → ↑ osteoporotic fracture risk, hypomagnesemia

children.label: Gastric Acid Secretion & Suppression › Somatostatin / Octreotide
children: MOA: inhibits histamine release (ECL cells) & gastrin release (G cells)
Octreotide (long-acting analog): treats gastrinoma / Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

children.label: Laxatives & Antidiarrheals
children: Type: Osmotic | Agents: Mg hydroxide/citrate, lactulose, PEG | MOA: Non-absorbable → draws water into lumen → distension → peristalsis
Type: Bulk-forming | Agents: Psyllium | MOA: Hydrophilic colloid absorbs water → distension → peristalsis
Type: Stool softener | Agents: Docusate | MOA: Surfactant → water/lipid penetration into stool
Type: Stimulant | Agents: Senna | MOA: Stimulates enteric nervous system & colonic secretion
Lactulose also treats hepatic encephalopathy: gut bacteria metabolize it → acidic metabolites → traps NH3 as NH4+ → excreted
Hepatic encephalopathy (cirrhosis, ↑ammonia) → asterixis (flapping tremor)
Rifaximin (poorly absorbed antibiotic): eradicates ammonia-producing gut flora → treats hepatic encephalopathy
Chronic senna use → melanosis coli
AE (laxatives, general): diarrhea, dehydration

children.label: Laxatives & Antidiarrheals › Antidiarrheals (opioid agonists)
children: Loperamide: mu-opioid agonist; does not cross BBB → no analgesia/addiction potential
Diphenoxylate: mu-opioid agonist, some BBB penetration → combined with atropine to deter abuse
MOA: activate mu-opioid receptors in GI tract → ↑ colonic phasic segmenting → ↑ transit time
Contraindicated with bloody diarrhea or fever (treat underlying cause)
VIPoma / carcinoid syndrome (secretory diarrhea) → treat with octreotide

children.label: Coagulation Cascade Basics
children: Factor Xa converts prothrombin (factor II) → thrombin
Thrombin converts fibrinogen → fibrin monomers → crosslinked (Ca2+, phospholipid, factor XIII) → stable fibrin clot

children.label: Heparins
children: Agent: Unfractionated heparin (UFH) | MOA: Binds antithrombin III → irreversibly inactivates thrombin AND factor Xa | Monitoring: aPTT | Notes: Reversed by protamine sulfate
Agent: LMWH | MOA: Binds antithrombin III → inhibits factor Xa >> thrombin | Monitoring: Not required | Notes: Longer half-life; lower HIT risk; protamine less effective
Agent: Fondaparinux | MOA: Binds antithrombin III (high specificity) → inhibits Xa only | Monitoring: — | Notes: Lowest HIT risk; protamine ineffective
Uses: DVT/PE prophylaxis & acute treatment; acute MI (prevents clot extension/formation); safe in pregnancy

AE (all heparins): bleeding (monitor PTT); HIT — antibodies vs. heparin–PF4 complex → paradoxical thrombosis despite low platelets; hypoaldosteronism (even at low dose) → type 4 RTA → hyperkalemia; osteoporosis
Direct thrombin inhibitors (argatroban, dabigatran, bivalirudin) → used in HIT
Direct factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban) → oral; long-term anticoagulation in AFib

children.label: Vitamin K & Warfarin
children: Vitamin K = cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X + proteins C & S
VKOR converts inactive vitamin K epoxide → active vitamin K
Warfarin inhibits VKOR → ↓ active vitamin K → ↓ functional II, VII, IX, X, protein C/S
Factor VII (shortest half-life) is reduced first
Onset 8–12h; full effect ~3 days → not for acute thrombotic events
Monitor: PT / INR (extrinsic pathway); goal INR 2–3
Use: long-term AFib anticoagulation, DVT prophylaxis (acute DVT treated with IV heparin first — warfarin has delayed onset)

AE: crosses placenta → teratogenic/hemorrhagic effects; early hypercoagulable state (protein C falls first) → warfarin-induced skin necrosis (esp. with protein C deficiency) → prevented by heparin bridge
Reversal: Vitamin K (delayed), FFP (immediate)
